functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population

neuromuscular_junction_zone.location_description: mid-belly endplate band -- for where this band lies along the muscle, see motor_endplate_zones

functional_compartments.function_note: 'Lat dorsi's little helper' -- shares the same insertion groove and internal-rotator/adductor/extensor action.
functional_compartments.source: Holzbaur KR, Murray WM, Delp SL (2005) Ann Biomed Eng 33(6):829-840 -- upper-extremity muscle architecture model (fascicle length, pennation, PCSA)

motor_endplate_zones.reference_line_to: insertion (crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus)
motor_endplate_zones.notes: Given by Yi et al. as the middle 20% of the muscle from origin to insertion.
motor_endplate_zones.source: Diaconu S et al. (Elias University Hospital), 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part II -- Proximal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(6):276 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17060276 -- review synthesis of the intramuscular neural arborization literature it cites (Yi, Li, Yang, Moon and others)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Transverse on the posterior thoracic wall 2-3 cm distal to the posterior axillary fold, with the shoulder held adducted and internally rotated.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Superficial to the rib cortex and intercostal muscles.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Three masses appear medial to lateral: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi.
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Injected with pectoralis major and subscapularis for the internally rotated, adducted shoulder, and with latissimus dorsi for the extended one. Also used for hemiplegic shoulder pain, where the deep pair (teres major, subscapularis) is injected alongside the superficial pair (pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi).
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Diaconu S et al. (Elias University Hospital), 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part II -- Proximal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(6):276 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17060276 -- review synthesis of the intramuscular neural arborization literature it cites (Yi, Li, Yang, Moon and others)

trigger_points.location_description: Medial trigger point near the inferior-angle origin of the muscle
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Posterior deltoid region and over the long head of triceps; occasionally to the dorsal forearm; rarely to the scapular area.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Sharp with reaching up-and-forward (driving, serving); limited end-range elevation (hand-up-the-back and full overhead reach both pull on it).
trigger_points.notes: The most frequent latent trigger-point muscle in chronic shoulder pain (49% of patients).
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (Donnelly JM, Fernandez-de-las-Penas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds), Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual, 3rd ed., Wolters Kluwer, 2019)

trigger_points.location_description: Lateral trigger point in the posterior axillary fold near the humeral insertion, pincer-palpated
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Posterior deltoid region and over the long head of triceps; occasionally to the dorsal forearm; rarely to the scapular area.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Sharp with reaching up-and-forward (driving, serving); limited end-range elevation (hand-up-the-back and full overhead reach both pull on it).

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); shoulder_muscles_reference_v1.html, compiled 31/08/2026. Sources policy: Gray’s Anatomy 43rd ed. (2026), Moore 9th ed., Neumann 3rd ed., Travell & Simons 3rd ed. (2019) and peer-reviewed journals only; 13 journal records re-retrieved via PubMed on 31/08/2026 (tagged), the rest flagged.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Internal rotation, adduction and extension of the humerus from flexion (“latissimus’ little helper”); active mainly against resistance and in pulling/climbing; stabilises the scapulo-humeral relationship at the inferior angle during elevation (it must lengthen for full flexion–abduction). Tightness restricts terminal elevation and drags the scapula into anterior tilt/rotation.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: Bursa between the teres major and latissimus tendons; a subtendinous bursa may separate the latissimus/teres complex from the humerus. Adjacent structures — mutual influence: Radial nerve and profunda brachii pass through the triangular interval at its lower border (entrapment/traction site); axillary nerve just above it; latissimus tendon anterior; long head of triceps crossing behind separates the spaces — hypertrophy (throwers) narrows both.

trigger_points.location: Two classic sites: medial TrP near the inferior-angle origin and a lateral TrP in the posterior axillary fold near the insertion (pincer-palpated). The most frequent latent TrP in chronic shoulder pain (49% of patients).
trigger_points.referred_pain: Posterior deltoid region and over the long head of triceps; occasionally to the dorsal forearm; rarely to the scapular area. Sharp with reaching up-and-forward (driving, serving).
trigger_points.source: Donnelly JM, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds). Travell, Simons & Simons’ Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual. 3rd ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2019. Muscle chapters as named in each section.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Into its felt zone (posterior deltoid/upper arm): subscapularis, teres minor, latissimus, triceps long head, posterior deltoid, levator scapulae
C6–C7 facet patterns reach the periscapular area.
clinical.movement_restrictions_aggravators: Limited end-range elevation (hand-up-the-back and full overhead reach both pull on it); stretch pain at terminal abduction–ER.
clinical.notes: In stiff shoulders with full passive ER at side but blocked terminal elevation, check teres major/latissimus tightness, not only the capsule.
clinical.caveat: Trigger-point locations and referral maps derive from the Travell–Simons clinical-observational tradition, now standardised by Delphi consensus criteria [32] and supported by prevalence and hyperalgesia studies in shoulder pain [30,31]; they are expert-level evidence, not trial-level, and inter-examiner reliability of TrP palpation is moderate. Facet, ACJ and subacromial referral patterns, by contrast, come from experimental provocation in volunteers/patients [33,34,37]. Textbook anatomy is cited at section level; where major texts disagree (segmental levels), the range is given and flagged. Figures and patterns older than 12 months are anatomical/physiological constants and are not considered stale.
